newsitem.title: ZAIRE: High expectations as Zaire awaits Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: High expectations as Zaire awaits Mobutu.

text.p: Zaire was preparing a mammoth welcome for veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko's return from Europe on Tuesday after months of cancer treatment during which the country has been torn by a Tutsi rebellion in the east.
State radio broadcast appeals on Monday to residents of Kinshasa to turn out in huge numbers for Mobutu, who arrives aboard his personal aircraft at around 3.0 p.m. (1400 GMT).

The 66-year-old Mobutu has ruled Zaire for 31 years, most of the time unchallenged. He has been away for more than three months, first for prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland and then recuperating at his luxury villa on the French Riviera.
A presidential press spokesman, Lumbana Kapasa, told reporters on Monday that Mobutu had interrupted his convalescence because the crisis in Zaire demanded his presence.
"Tomorrow he will be addressing the nation and he will say what is going to happen and why he has returned to Zaire despite his convalescence," Lumbana told a news briefing in the capital.

After welcoming ceremonies at Njili International Airport, Mobutu will return to his fortified hilltop residence from where he is due to address the nation in a televised speech at 5 p.m. (1600 GMT), Lumbana said.
Rwandan-backed ethnic Tutsis who took up arms in October have seized a strip of borderland, and now say their objective is to overthrow Mobutu, whose army has failed to halt the guerrillas.

The refugee crisis and regional security problems triggered by unrest in Zaire and neighbouring Burundi were discussed at a summit in Kenya on Monday attended by South African President Nelson Mandela and eight other African leaders.
Mandela, succumbing to international pressure to get involved, was taking part in high-level talks on the conflicts for the first time. Zaire was absent, Kenyan officials said.
The pro-Mobutu Kinshasa newspaper The Soft said the president would stay in the capital for two or three weeks and would then return to France to continue his convalescence under medical supervision.
Government and presidential officials have declined to specify how long Mobutu will stay in Zaire.
It will be the first time the president has visited the capital since January, when he toured the site of a plane crash that killed more than 300 people.
Since the beginning of a six-year political transition to democracy in 1990, he has preferred to remain in his jungle palace of Gbadolite in the northern Equateur Region.
Local newspapers of all political shades have indulged in wild speculation on the implications of Mobutu's return, and whether it could herald changes in the government and the military.
The more radical of his opponents blame his rule since seizing power as a young army officer in 1965 for the current crisis in Zaire, and say his return will only make matters worse.

However even these opponents believe that as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Mobutu is the only man able to boost morale in the defeated army and re-shuffle the high command in preparation for a counter-offensive.
